title: Popularity Cache
statement: Design a cache with room for capacity entries that evicts the least frequently used key when full. Every get of a present key and every put counts as a use of that key. When several keys tie for the lowest use count, evict the one used least recently. Operations arrive as ["put", key, value] or ["get", key]. A put of an existing key updates its value (and counts as a use). Return the results of every get in order: the stored value, or -1 if the key is absent.
constraints: Keys and values are integers from -1000000 through 1000000

examples.explanation: Key 2 (used once) is evicted for 3. When 4 arrives, keys 1 and 3 both have two uses; 1 was used less recently, so it is evicted.

hints.content: Each key needs a value, a use count and a recency.
Scanning every entry to find the victim on each eviction costs O(capacity).
Group keys by use count: one ordered collection per count, oldest first.
Track the smallest use count currently present. Using a key moves it from its count's group to the end of the next count's group.
A new key always has count 1, so after inserting one, the smallest count is 1. JavaScript's Set keeps insertion order, which gives 'least recently used within a count' for free.

testCases.explanation: Key 2 (used once) is evicted for 3. When 4 arrives, keys 1 and 3 both have two uses; 1 was used less recently, so it is evicted.
Capacity 1 always evicts the previous key.
Updating key 1 counts as a use, so key 2 is evicted.
All tied at two uses: the least recently used (1) is evicted.
Gets of missing keys do not count as uses.
A long workload where scanning all entries on each eviction is slow.

solutions.title: Scan for the victim
solutions.intuition: Store counts and last-use times, and search all entries when you must evict.
solutions.approach: Keep a Map of key → {value, uses, last}. On eviction, scan for the smallest (uses, last).
solutions.pseudocode: tick++ per op; get: update uses/last; put new when full: evict argmin(uses, last); insert with uses = 1
commonMistakes: Breaking frequency ties arbitrarily instead of by recency.
Counting a failed get as a use.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Recording counts and timestamps and scanning on eviction is correct and easy to verify, but eviction is linear in the capacity.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: put 3 when full: the minimum uses is key 2 → evict.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.content: Later, 1 and 3 tie at 2 uses; 1 has the older last use → evict 1 for 4.

solutions.title: Frequency buckets with a minimum pointer
solutions.intuition: Ordered groups per use count make the victim the first key of the lowest non-empty group, which a single minimum pointer tracks.
solutions.approach: values: key → value; freq: key → count; buckets: count → Set of keys in recency order; minFreq. touch(key) moves the key to count + 1 and bumps minFreq if its old bucket emptied and was the minimum. A new key evicts the first key of buckets[minFreq] when full, then enters bucket 1 and sets minFreq = 1.
solutions.pseudocode:
get k: if absent -1; touch(k); return value
put k,v: if present: set; touch; return
  if full: evict first of buckets[minFreq]
  insert with freq 1 into buckets[1]; minFreq = 1
commonMistakes: Forgetting to advance minFreq when the minimum bucket empties during touch.
Leaving empty buckets behind, so the victim lookup finds an empty set.
solutions.interviewExplanation: I keep a bucket of keys per use count, each an insertion-ordered Set so its first key is the least recently used at that count, plus a minFreq pointer. A use moves the key up one bucket and adjusts minFreq only if it emptied the minimum bucket. A new key always resets minFreq to 1. Everything is O(1). In languages without ordered sets, each bucket would be a doubly linked list with a map from key to node.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: After the first five operations: buckets {1: [3], 2: [1]}, minFreq 1.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.content: put 4 when full evicts the first of bucket 2 (key 1), then inserts 4 at count 1.
